Stuart Robinson
stō'ərt rob'in-sən
n. (Stuart Robinson, 1814–1881, Irish-born Kentucky Presbyterian pastor and theologian of the spiritual independence of the church)
English patronymic Robin-son, son of Robert.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Stuart Robinson was born in Ireland, raised in Virginia, and became the clearest American voice for the doctrine that the church is a kingdom of a different order than the state. His book The Church of God as an Essential Element of the Gospel argued that the visible church is not a voluntary society formed by men for religious ends but an institution founded by Christ with its own constitution, officers, and jurisdiction, and that it therefore has no commission to legislate on civil questions. He held the Louisville pulpit, edited the True Presbyterian, and when wartime authorities moved against him he spent four years in Canada rather than submit his pulpit to a political test. He returned and served Louisville until his death. His position was not indifference to public righteousness but a refusal to let the church spend its one commission — Mat 28:19, the teaching of what Christ commanded — on business Christ had not given it. Act 20:27 was his measure of a minister: whether he had declared all the counsel of God, and nothing besides.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the church as a congregation of Christians, and jurisdiction as the legal power of governing within defined limits.

expand to see more

CHURCH, n. A congregation of Christians united under one form of ecclesiastical government, in one creed, and using the same ritual and ceremonies.

JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.

SPIRIT'UAL, a. Consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal. Pertaining to the renewed nature of man.

Key Scripture

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Act 20:27 — "For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God."

1Ti 3:15 — "But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth."

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Modern Corruption

The church is a kingdom with its own charter, and a minister who legislates beyond it has left his commission.

expand to see more

Robinson wrote against two errors at once, and both are still with us. The first is Erastian: the state assumes authority over the church's worship, officers, and teaching, which is what drove him to Canada. The second is the church's own overreach, in which assemblies bind consciences on matters Scripture has not addressed and then treat dissent as impiety. 1Ti 3:15 names the church “the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — of the truth, which is a bounded commission, not an unbounded one.

The dictionary holds Robinson's principle while refusing the use later made of it. Spiritual independence was invoked in the American South to silence the church on manstealing, which Scripture names outright in the list at 1Ti 1:10 and sentences at Exo 21:16. A doctrine that forbids the church to legislate where Scripture is silent cannot be stretched to forbid her to speak where Scripture is loud. Robinson's rule, honestly applied, obliged the church to preach Exo 21:16; his section of the church did not, and the failure was theirs, not the doctrine's.

"“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — the one commission."
